topic: Bulk and surface properties of matter including nanoparticles (chemistry only)
subject: chemistry

items.q: Which particles have diameters between 1 x 10⁻⁷ m and 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m?
items.correct: Fine particles, which are known as PM2.5
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'fine' is the smallest grade of anything - fine sand, fine flour - so students rank the categories by the sound of the word instead of by the diameters printed beside them. Rank them by the numbers the specification gives: nanoparticles 1–100 nm, fine particles 100 to 2500 nm, coarse particles up to 1 x 10⁻⁵ m. 'Fine' is only fine compared with dust.

items.q: A particle in smoke is measured and found to have a diameter of 5 x 10⁻⁶ m. Which class of particle is it?
items.correct: A coarse particle, often called dust
items.why: Every other size in this topic is quoted in nanometres, so students assume the PM numbers must be nanometres too. That makes both PM classes look smaller than nanoparticles, reversing the whole size order. The PM numbers are in micrometres. PM2.5 is 2500 nm and PM₁₀ is 10 000 nm, so both classes are far larger than any nanoparticle.
items.random_wrong: A fine particle, only about 5 nm wide

items.q: The side of a cube of a solid is decreased by a factor of 10. What happens to its surface area to volume ratio?
items.correct: It increases by a factor of 10
items.misconception: It decreases by a factor of ten
items.why: Students track the surface area alone and forget that the volume is falling faster than the area. Everything about the cube is getting smaller, so the ratio 'must' get smaller as well. Surface area falls by 100 but volume falls by 1000, so area ÷ volume rises tenfold. For a cube of side l the ratio is 6 ÷ l, which grows as l shrinks.
items.random_wrong: It increases by one hundred times

items.q: A cube of side 1 cm has a surface area to volume ratio of 6. What is the ratio for a cube of side 0.1 cm?
items.why: The words 'surface area to volume' are read as a fraction with volume on top, or the two numbers are simply divided in whichever order gives a tidier-looking answer. The quantity named first goes on top: surface area ÷ volume. For a 1 cm cube that is 6 ÷ 1 = 6.

items.q: Nanoparticles of a metal can behave differently from a lump of the same metal. Why?
items.correct: They have a much higher surface area to volume ratio
items.misconception: They are a more reactive element than the metal
items.why: A change of property is assumed to require a chemical change, so students invent a new substance rather than accept that one substance can behave differently at a different size. The material is chemically identical - same element or compound, same formula. Only the surface area to volume ratio has changed, and that alone is enough to change the properties.
items.random_wrong: They are built from different atoms than the lump

items.q: A sun cream can be made using a metal oxide in bulk form or as nanoparticles of the same oxide. Compared with the bulk form, the mass of the nanoparticle form needed to protect the skin is:
items.correct: smaller, as far more surface gets exposed
items.misconception: larger, since each particle is so very tiny
items.why: Students count particles rather than weighing them. It is true that far more particles are needed, but each one has almost no mass, so the total mass still falls. Compare masses, not particle counts. A gram of nanoparticles offers vastly more surface than a gram of the bulk solid, so less material does the same job.
items.random_wrong: the same, because the oxide is unchanged

items.q: A typical atom has a diameter of about 0.1 nm. Roughly how many atoms would fit across a structure 1 nm wide?
items.correct: About ten atoms in a row
items.why: The atomic diameter is misremembered as a picometre-scale number, so the gap between the nanoscale and the atomic scale is inflated by a factor of a thousand. Take an atom as roughly 0.1 nm, that is 1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m. Divide 1 nm by 0.1 nm and you get about ten atoms across.

items.q: A nanoparticle is 20 nm across. A typical atom is about 0.1 nm across. Roughly how many atoms lie along one edge of the nanoparticle?
items.why: 'Nano' is used loosely to mean 'as small as things get', and students meet 10⁻⁹ m and 10⁻¹⁰ m in the same breath, so the two scales collapse into one. One atom is roughly 0.1 nm, so even the smallest 1 nm structure is about ten atoms across, and a nanoparticle holds a few hundred atoms.

items.q: Which list gives only applications of nanoparticles named in the specification?
items.correct: Medicine, electronics, sun creams, deodorants, catalysts
items.misconception: Fertilisers, road salt, cement, alloys, and water pipes
items.why: A change of property is assumed to require a chemical change, so students invent a new substance rather than accept that one substance can behave differently at a different size. The material is chemically identical - same element or compound, same formula. Only the surface area to volume ratio has changed, and that alone is enough to change the properties.
items.random_wrong: Research laboratories and specialised university work

items.q: A sun cream made with nanoparticles of a metal oxide is clear on the skin and blocks more ultraviolet light than the bulk form, but its long-term effects on skin cells have not yet been fully tested. Which is the best evaluation?
items.correct: Better protection and appearance, but long-term effects untested
items.misconception: It should be used, since being on sale proves it is safe
items.why: Being on sale is taken as proof of complete safety, and because these materials are new, long-term evidence has simply not had time to accumulate. The specification asks you to explain that there are possible risks. Being in use shows a product met current rules, not that every long-term effect is known.
items.random_wrong: It should be used, because it blocks the most ultraviolet light

items.q: A factory can buy a catalyst as 5 kg of pellets or as 50 g of nanoparticles that speed the reaction just as much. The nanoparticle form costs more per gram. Which evaluation uses this information best?
items.correct: Much less mass is needed, so a higher price per gram may pay off
items.misconception: Neither wins, as the reactive nanoparticles wear out fast
items.why: 'More effective' is heard as 'more reactive', and the definition of a catalyst as unchanged at the end of the reaction is forgotten under the pressure of an unfamiliar context. A catalyst is not used up at all. Splitting it into nanoparticles simply exposes far more surface for the reaction, so a smaller mass is needed.
items.random_wrong: Nanoparticles are better, since they are used up faster

items.q: Why do scientists say there are possible risks in using nanoparticles?
items.correct: They may enter cells and effects are not known
items.misconception: They are on sale already, which proves they are safe
items.why: Being on sale is taken as proof of complete safety, and because these materials are new, long-term evidence has simply not had time to accumulate. The specification asks you to explain that there are possible risks. Being in use shows a product met current rules, not that every long-term effect is known.
items.random_wrong: They are far too small to affect the body's cells

items.q: By what factor does the surface area to volume ratio change when the side is divided by 10?
items.correct: It increases by a factor of 10.
items.misconception: It increases by a factor of 100, because surface area depends on the square of the side.
items.why: The 6l² in the surface area formula is the most memorable part, so students apply the squaring rule to the ratio itself and never divide by the l³ underneath it. Work with the whole ratio: 6l² ÷ l³ = 6 ÷ l. Only one power of l survives, so dividing the side by 10 multiplies the ratio by 10, not by 100.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.correct: In medicine, in electronics, in cosmetics and sun creams, as deodorants, and as catalysts.
items.misconception: Nanoparticles are only used in research laboratories and have no uses in ordinary consumer products.
items.why: The word 'nanotechnology' sounds futuristic and experimental, so students file it under research only and overlook the sun cream and the deodorant already in the bathroom. The specification lists everyday uses: medicine, electronics, cosmetics and sun creams, deodorants and catalysts. New applications are also an important area of research.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What must an evaluation of a use of nanoparticles include?
items.correct: Both the advantages and the disadvantages given, and a judgement that refers to both of them.
items.misconception: An evaluation means listing every advantage you can find and then recommending the use.
items.why: Students treat 'evaluate' as 'justify', so the answer becomes one-sided: only the supporting evidence in the stem is used and the drawbacks printed alongside it are read past. Use the information on both sides, weigh one against the other, and state a conclusion that acknowledges the cost as well as the benefit.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why does the small size of nanoparticles create a possible risk?
items.correct: They are small enough to be breathed deep into the lungs or to pass into cells, where their effects are not fully known.
items.misconception: Nanoparticles are far too small to have any effect on the body, so they simply pass straight through it.
items.why: Small is equated with harmless. Because a nanoparticle is invisible, students assume the body cannot notice it, which reverses the actual concern that it reaches places larger particles cannot. It is the small size that causes the concern: nanoparticles can reach parts of the body that coarse particles never reach, and their high surface area makes them chemically active there.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.2.4 Bulk and surface properties of matter including nanoparticles (chemistry only)
